title: Lesson 39: Transaction Lifecycle: State, Save Order, and the 4 Trigger Contexts in One Transaction
description: The fixed sequence a record save walks from load to commit, what lives in the database versus in memory at each phase, and the four trigger contexts one transaction can run.

questions.question: Per the lesson “Transaction Lifecycle: State, Save Order, and the 4 Trigger Contexts in One Transaction”, an after update trigger updates a field on the same record it was fired for. What does that cost and trigger?
options: Nothing extra, because after context writes to Trigger.new without spending a DML statement.
One DML statement, but the save order is not re-entered because the record is already in the database.
A DML statement against the transaction budget plus a full re-entry into the save order from step 1, which fires the record’s update triggers again.
An automatic rollback of the transaction, because an after trigger may not modify the record it was fired for.
questions.explanation: After context exists to touch records that need the saved Id or were not part of the original DML, and a write back to the same record restarts the sequence.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson’s guidance?
options: Roll-up summary fields recalculate near the end of the save order, after after triggers have run, so an after trigger that reads a parent’s roll-up is reading the pre-recalculation value.
Before triggers run after custom validation rules, so a validation rule can never see a value a before trigger set.
Values written to Trigger.new in a before trigger each cost a DML statement against the budget.
A workflow field update re-fires update triggers without limit, which is why the platform has to cap it at one extra pass.
questions.explanation: Roll-up recalculation happens well after after triggers, which is why sequencing bugs rather than logic bugs are the usual cause of a stale number.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: A record save that touches only one operation runs all four save contexts.

A batch that upserts 5,000 leads runs before insert, before update, after insert, and after update inside the single transaction, so insert-only logic misreads the updates as if they were new records.
Dispatching on System.TriggerOperation is discouraged in favor of chaining Trigger.isBefore and Trigger.isInsert checks.
An unhandled exception rolls back only the Apex work in the current phase, leaving the later phases to complete.
questions.explanation: A transaction is not limited to one DML statement or one operation, so a mixed upsert exercises all four contexts and a trigger has to dispatch on the operation type rather than assume it.
